image_description:
1. **Chart type**  
   - Overlaid stepped area chart / cumulative distribution-style area chart.

2. **Layout techniques**  
   - Uses **overlaid filled areas** with transparency-like layering by color.
   - No faceting or small multiples.
   - Not stacked to sum categories at each x-position; instead, multiple cumulative areas are layered on the same axes.

3. **Data variables**

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Estimated cumulative force of head hits | Quantitative | Position on x-axis |
| Percent of players studied | Quantitative | Position on y-axis |
| C.T.E. stage / diagnosis category (No C.T.E., Stage 1 C.T.E., Stage 2, Stage 3, Stage 4) | Categorical/ordinal | Color/hue of filled area; legend |

**Visible category labels in legend:** No C.T.E., Stage 1 C.T.E., Stage 2, Stage 3, Stage 4.

Answer the following questions
What do you notice?
One thing I notice is that the more cultivated force the head is hit with, the more the stage of C.T.E a football player is going to have. The graph supports this because it shows that if there is more force, players have gotten stage 4 C.T.E. Also, most of the players who have been hit with less force, are at lower stages and even no C.T.E.
What do you wonder?
I wonder if the players who were studded had different helmets, with different levels of protection. If someone was to be hit while wearing a helmet with less padding, then someone with a more padded helmet, they would probably be more at risk to get C.T.E. 
How does this relate to you and your community?
This is useful in my community because it is such a football focused area. Using these statistics, we can find more ways to make football safer and more enjoyable. To be able to play without thinking of the consequences if you were hit in the wrong spot would be the most ideal circumstance. 
What is going on in this graph?
This graph is measuring how much force a head can be hit with and how it leads to a football player getting different stages of C.T.E. 
Headline: How much can football players take in the head before it is too much and they are left with CTE?

I notice that in the graph, more cumulative force creates more stage 4 head traumas. As you go towards the right of the graph we start to see more Stage 3s and 4s as the cumulative force increases. This shows that over time as the force of the head impacts adds up, the stage level of CTE does too. I also notice that the growth of cumulative force doesn't directly correlate with the chances of injury, sometimes there are even dropping rates of C.T.E on higher cumulative force. For example, at the end side of the graph it goes from 100% experiencing some form of C.T.E to only 60% on a higher force. 

I wonder if the impacts of helmets play a factor in this study? I also wonder how many blows an athlete can take before seeing signs of the different stages of CTE and if there’s medical help that can help prevent the symptoms? How long has each player been playing football for? 


This does not impact me directly but in my school community, a large percentage of boys play football at school. These alarming statistics of CTE injuries makes me worry for the boys at school and I wonder if these head injuries affect their academic abilities. 

The graph shows the estimated cumulative force of head hits for 631 former football players. 
“CTE v Football Players: How dangerous is football?”

comments.raw_comment:
This graph shows the cumulative force of head hits for 631 former football players and how that affected their  CTE. From this graph, I observe that more cumulative force usually creates greater head trauma, and less curative force results in less head trauma. CTE or chronic traumatic encephalopathy is associated with repeated blows to the head. Therefore it can be assumed that the more traumatic these hits are the more damage they will cause. I wonder if there is a direct correlation between the severity of the disease in the symptoms of memory loss, depression, aggressive behavior, and, sometimes, suicidal thoughts. This graph further demonstrates how unpredictable CTE can be at times. For example, if someone is hit with middle-level cumulative force they could have anywhere from no CTE at all to extremely severe stage 4 CTE. This could be a seriously life-changing difference for someone. However, there is a clear trend within the graph that directly relates more force with a greater CTE and less force with minor or no CTE. I really hope that this graph reaches the right audience and spreads awareness of contact sports such as football and boxing where head injuries are common. I also hope that this leaves an impact on people so much so that there become more regulations and/or head protective gear in these sports to try and prevent severe CTE for players, especially teens who will suffer the long-term effects.
“Watch Out Head Trauma Coming Your Way!”

comments.raw_comment:
This graph depicts how head injuries have gravely impacted football players, specifically regarding chronic traumatic encephalopathy. Chronic traumatic encephalopathy, C.T.E. for short, a brain disease that can result from repeated trauma to the head, is currently both incurable and fatal. According to this graph, the more head trauma a football player experiences, the more likely they are to suffer from C.T.E. While C.T.E. can cause illnesses such as dementia, it has also been deteriorating mental health. Former players, Junior Seau, Philip Adams, and Dave Duerson, all diagnosed with severe depression from C.T.E., took their own lives. Aaron Hernandez and Jovan Belcher, both players suffering from C.T.E., were described as growing violent before commiting murder. I wonder why C.T.E., being such a pressing issue, is it not being discussed and researched more. Though this graph correlates brain injuries in football to chronic traumatic encephalopathy, this disease can be brought about by any high-contact sport. In my community, most people play or have played an intensive sport where concussions are prevalent. I have witnessed athletes be rushed to the hospital after serious head blows in sports ranging from soccer to cheerleading. As athletes in all sports continue to push the limits harder each year, will I have to worry about my teenage friends developing a life-threatening brain disease?

“What Is More Important: Pigskin or Your Life?”

I wonder why there are there is so much variety in the degree of force applied and the stage of CTE. The numbers may be affected by whether the player has experienced CTE in the past. Then, their condition would be exacerbated. 

This relates to my community because football is a popular American pastime. Athletes are receiving debilitating injuries for (often) a brief sporting career. This relates to me because, if I ever receive head hits, I will know that there is a possibility of CTE.

The next graph release will be published on Friday with live moderation in TWO weeks on Wednesday, October 18.  The topic – the New York Times’ Spelling Bee – puzzle or is it a game?

1. The first few things I notice are the main colors and how they increase with more hard hitting, but also the blank spot in the red. I find this anomaly extremely confusing and conclude it to be basic luck by the players that have suffered many head injuries, yet not end up with CTE. It does show that the people who have hit their head with the most cumulative force are always getting the worst cases of CTE and the people who get hit with the least cumulative force don’t get the worst type of CTE and over 50% don’t even get CTE at all.
2. The anomaly part of the graph where there is a section of people getting hit with more cumulative force, yet don’t get CTE is the part that interests me the most. This seems to be one of those weird things that happens where someone smokes and drinks their entire life and ends up living till their 90’s, something that just can happen by some sort of miracle. I think that this part of the graph just goes to show the weird possibilities human bodies can accomplish. 
3. This affects my community because football is played by people our age, meaning that people that haven’t even gotten to college could be getting CTE. I find that this is very dangerous and I feel that we should be finding a way to minimize injury in this sport until it dwindles down once people realize how weird it is to watch people just hit each other for a job. 
4. Catchy Title: CTE–Is It Really Worth It?

This data relates to myself and my community because of C.T.E. long lasting effects on the brain. For the people in my community who play football or other contact sports, C.T.E. damage is very real and dangerous.

A title for this could be "The Dark Truth of Sunday Night Fun: Brain Disease in Football"

comments.raw_comment:
I notice that C.T.E. seems to be very common in football players who endured head trauma, regardless of the force of the hits. Over 1/3 of the players with the less forceful head hits still developed C.T.E. As I look toward the middle of the x-axis, the numbers of players with C.T.E. nearly triple. As cumulative force of head hits increases, the numbers of C.T.E. skyrocket. This disease seems almost inevitable for football players experiencing repetitive head trauma (which occurs often in the sport). I wonder what percentage of former NFL players have C.T.E., I think it is worthwhile to do a similar study with a much larger population in order to better grasp the amount of players C.T.E. affects/affected. If the number is concerning, more awareness could be brought to this disease and preventative measures could be taken. This relates to me and my community because I watch football very often in the fall and winter. I see players experience head hits that could possibly lead to C.T.E. later down the line. Knowing the true scale and implications of this disease makes me not want to watch football as it lends itself to traumatic head injuries and I do not want to support something that is causing so much widespread harm. I hope that others in my community would feel similarly if they knew more about C.T.E., and I am sure that many parents would discourage their children from participating in football.

comments.raw_comment: In this graph, it is measuring the correlation between the amount of force applied to football players’ heads when hit and the stage of C.T.E. that they experienced. Additionally, the graph also measures the percentage of players who received a certain stage of C.T.E. When reading the x-axis of the graph, it demonstrates that the left hand side represents when there was less cumulative force applied to the players. When less cumulative force was applied, most players had either no C.T.E. or stage 1 C.T.E. However, the x-axis shows that the right hand side represents when more cumulative force was applied and it appears that 100% of players had stage 4 C.T.E. as the graph goes further right. This data shows how there is a positive correlation between the amount of force applied and the stage of C.T.E.. I wonder what measures might be in place to try to prevent C.T.E. injuries in football players and how they can be altered to make injury prevention more efficient. This relates to my community because I know many football players, and it is important for them to be educated on the dangers of football and C.T.E. injuries to maintain safety on the field. My headline for this graph would be: “Uncovering the Dangers Behind Football - Should Players Take the Risk?”

comments.raw_comment: I noticed that in the graph, the more the cumulative force of blows to the head during football, the higher the chance there is of chronic traumatic encephalopathy, or C.T.E., a degenerative brain disease caused by a continuous amount of trauma induced to the head, which in this graph is displayed by sports accidents. Football, I’ve learned, is a very high-impact sport with great risk and plenty of injuries. Being a contact sport, it comes with the probability of sustaining dangerous injuries- head injuries. I wonder why some people tend to continue playing that specific sport after such injuries are induced, but I can understand that as a fellow athlete, it is difficult to walk away from your sport when you need to or have to due to injury. I have seen many football-related injuries in my years of high school or heard about certain severities of ones in the past, and have come to an understanding that football is more dangerous than I had suspected. I am not someone who enjoys football or watching sports in general, and I only run cross country and track, so mine aren’t contact sports at all (unless you count the occasional shove at the starting line). A good headline for this substantial and informative graph on head injuries in football would be “The Greater The Force, The Worse The Risk.” We should probably have more prevention of this disease and other high-impact injury protection protocols in this sport.

comments.raw_comment: The data in the graph demonstrates how the force of heads hit for 631 football players is related to the stage of a concussion. The x-axis of the graph depicts the extremity of the brain disease, C.T.E in correlation to the amount of force applied (stage 1 being of lesser extremity and stage 4 as a more extreme form of C.T.E). With this information, I noticed that the greater cumulative force applied to the head, the more likely the C.T.E was at stage 3 or 4, or very severe and had the possibility of deeper internal injury. This applies vice-versa, where the less cumulative force means a greater chance of a lower form of C.T.E (or none at all). I wonder if the people that conducted the research group to examine C.T.E now advise people against playing football (because of the risk of severe head injury). I also wonder how an area or region of the brain that was hit with force impacted the stage of C.T.E. This graph relates to my community because it serves as a warning to those that play football or other sports that may involve force to the head. This is because it can influence people to wear proper protective gear and know the risks of playing. A headline that captures the graph’s main idea is: “Warning: The Dangers of Football"

comments.raw_comment:
1. Analyzing the graph, based on the cumulative force of head hits from 631 former football players, as the head hits with cultivating force progressively increase, Football players are shown to be more prone to reaching dangerous stages of C.T.E. While less cultivating force demonstrates that a minor of those who were studied suffered from C.T.E., as the force gradually increases, 20% to 100% of players whose brains were studied, were confirmed to have subsequently shown stages of C.T.E. Many of these were shown to be in stages 3 and 4 (shown in brown and dark red). 

2. I wonder whether the statistics shown, manage to shift parent's viewpoints in letting their children participate in this rough sport, which could potentially harm their children in the long run. Will new rules be established to minimize the harm in football? Will there be more safety gear? What will the numbers look like for those suffering from C.T.E. due to football in the years to come?


3. Being in a community and in a family that takes a part in and is big on football, there are always players who suffer from an injury in a game, whether it's a concussion or a sprained muscle. Every one of these players is at risk of getting C.T.E. In particular those training at young ages like 10-11, whose brains are even more delicate and vulnerable to these head injuries.      

Title: From Booms and Clashes to a Severe Case of C.T.E, Is The Touchdown Worth The Risk?

1. I notice that higher stages of CTE relate to cumulative head hits from former football players. The lower force results in a less progressive, if not no CTE at all, while the higher cumulative force leads to CTE and higher stages of it, as seen by the percentage of former football players that had a severe case of CTE being low in the lower amounts of cumulative force. In contrast, higher amounts of force led to a higher percentage of football players to have it. 

2. I wonder from this graph at length of time do symptoms appear if it is only after hits cease to come to the head. Furthermore, the force aspect of the graph also makes me wonder how they calculated the cumulative force. Was it from nerve damage or overall damage to the brain? Is it the repeated blows or overall force? If it was this common in this many previous football players; how many have it now?
 
3. This affects my community as the football community within Perth Amboy is extremely strong, with it being many a person’s choice of sport right next to baseball. The fact that this degenerative disease is more likely to occur with something so common in the popular sport is alarming. It brings awareness to better safety gear to prevent this degenerative brain disease.
 
4. AAUGH! Hits To The Head Spell Danger for Football Athletes

comments.raw_comment: Football is a relatively dangerous sport, given how many players suffer from head injuries on average. A C.T.E., or Chronic traumatic encephalopathy, is a traumatic brain injury like a concussion. Football encourages players to tackle other players with extreme force to knock them down or remove obstacles. There is little control over how a person falls once they are hit, but how they are hit absolutely determines how badly they are injured. 100% of players who were hit with extreme force got a stage 4 C.T.E. upon impact on the ground. I notice how night numbers of players have received severe head trauma from the sport, but there is little education on how to prevent those injuries. Being hit with extreme force will lead to injury, but in the heat of the game, players are not actively thinking about injury prevention, only winning. I wonder why there is not more of an emphasis on safety in football. While players do wear padding, they are still praised for hard hits and tackles are a main part of the entertainment in TV coverage. It is upsetting to see how dangerous it is because of how popular the sport is for Americans both play and watch. With events like the Super Bowl, it is easy to forget how dangerous the game is for the players. We encourage good tackles and wild plays, but in reality, the safety of the players should be the most important part. The graph is showing the “Unmentioned dangers of Football” by exhibiting statistics of real injuries.

comments.raw_comment:
1. The graph illustrates head collisions with either more or less force. You can tell that with more cumulative force the 60% of the players will suffer between Stage 3-4 C.T.E.. You can also see that out of the 631 former footballers majority will receive at least a stage of C.T.E..   This is depressing to see, the odds of getting C.T.E. is more likely to happen if you do ever end up playing. 

2. This makes me wonder what more protection will organizations like the NFL put on players to make it safer to play. Although there are already helmets and pads to take the impact they are not fully efficient. In the future will helmets be sustainable and renewable to be efficient enough to take hits. If not more inventions should be thought of to remove the risk of receiving C.T.E..

3. At our middle school the motivational speaker Eric Legrand payed a visit talking about his situation. I remember how he explained he hit his head on the ground while playing football causing him to be paralyzed from the neck down. He began receiving care and rehabilitation which nursed him back to health. He left the lesson that since he never gave up neither should we.

4. How do we ensure the safety of football players? Does protection stop at helmets?

comments.raw_comment:
I notice that football players who absorb more cumulative force of head impacts develop higher stages of CTE. Towards the beginning of the graph we see the group of football players who absorbed less cumulative force of head impacts and there is mostly no CTE with only a couple of Stage 1s and 2s. But as you go towards the right of the graph we start to see more Stage 3s and 4s as the cumulative force absorbed increases. This shows that over time as the force of the head impacts adds up, the stage level of CTE increases.

I wonder why some of the cumulative force of head impacts doesn't affect others. Towards the very right of the graph, the gray is very distinctive. In a sea of red and orange, the gray sticks out as it shows a group of football players who experienced a good amount of head impacts had no CTE at all. This is interesting because why do they have no CTE even though they have enough cumulative force of head impacts to develop Stage 4 CTE?

This relates to me and my community as CTE is a very serious problem in schools. Parents are concerned about allowing their children to play football as it's a very physical sport and they don't want their children to get hurt. Learning about CTE and the amount of head impacts it takes to develop CTE can help us, as a community, to keep our football players safe on the field.

CTE: When Is It One Too Many Hits?
